opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'm proud of them mainly because of the problem they go after together, not any one of them alone.

Video generation has advanced very quickly, but most of that progress has come from scaling: bigger diffusion models, more compute, longer inference. You get beautiful clips, but they can take minutes on a cluster of GPUs. At Qualcomm we ask a different question: how do you make generative video practical, efficient, and controllable enough to eventually run close to the user, even on a device?

So these papers work on three pieces of that puzzle. The first is efficiency: cutting the cost of the denoising process through smarter sampling, fewer steps, and attention mechanisms that don't blow up quadratically with frame count and resolution. The second is temporal consistency. Single frames that look great aren't enough. Objects need to keep their identity, motion needs to be physically plausible, and you can't have flicker or drift over time. The third is control: letting users steer the generation with things like motion cues, layouts, or edits, instead of only a text prompt and hoping for the best.

What makes me especially proud is that this work comes from a fairly lean team competing at a venue where some groups have orders of magnitude more compute. Getting three papers accepted on such a crowded topic shows that algorithmic insight still matters, and that you don't need brute force to move the field forward. It also fits our broader belief that generative AI will be truly useful when it's efficient and personal, and that's what we're building toward.

r001.rationale: The response says the work aims to make video generation practical and eventually run close to users, even on a device, but does not state that the three papers enable models to run locally on consumer devices.

r002.rationale: It mentions attention mechanisms that avoid quadratic scaling, but does not identify changing where attention is applied as an acceleration method.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: Well, thanks for having me. I think what makes me proud is less about any single result and more about what the three papers together say about where we're going. If you look at the video generation space right now, the headline numbers all come from enormous models running in a datacenter, and the implicit assumption is that this is a cloud-only workload. We wanted to challenge that assumption from three different angles at once.

One paper is really about efficiency at the architecture level, making the diffusion backbone itself much cheaper, so the compute per frame drops dramatically without giving up temporal consistency, which is the thing that usually falls apart first when you shrink these models. The second one tackles the sampling side, cutting the number of denoising steps you need so the latency actually becomes something a person would tolerate interactively. And the third is about controllability, giving the user real handles on motion and content rather than just a text prompt and hoping for the best.

What I love is that these weren't done in isolation. The teams were talking to each other, and the results compound. When you put them together you start to see a path toward video generation that can actually run on a phone or an edge device, with your data staying on the device, with low latency, and with the kind of interactivity that makes it a creative tool rather than a slot machine.

And honestly, the other reason I'm proud is the people. These are papers coming out of a group that has to think about real constraints, memory, power, thermal budgets, and still produce work that stands up at CVPR against labs that don't have those constraints at all. That combination of rigor and practicality is exactly what I want our research to be known for.

r001.rationale: The response says the combined work creates a path to video generation running on a phone or edge device, with data staying on the device.

r002.rationale: It describes a cheaper diffusion backbone and fewer denoising steps, but does not identify changing where attention is applied as an acceleration method.

astra-6.text:
What makes me particularly proud is that video generation requires us to bring several difficult pieces together. Generating a compelling individual frame is one thing; maintaining consistency as objects move and the scene evolves is another. And then you have to think about the computational cost of doing that over many frames.

For us at Qualcomm, that efficiency question is especially important. We want to advance the quality of generative AI while also making it practical to use. So having three papers at CVPR is exciting as recognition of the team’s work, but the bigger motivation is moving toward video generation that is both capable and computationally accessible.

sol-6.1.text:
What makes me particularly proud is that we’re tackling both the quality of video generation and the efficiency needed to make it practical. With video, generating a beautiful individual frame isn’t enough—you need consistent appearance and coherent motion over time, and that becomes computationally expensive very quickly.

These three papers represent complementary efforts toward that challenge. For us at Qualcomm, the exciting question is how we can bring these capabilities closer to the user, within real compute and power constraints. Having that work accepted at CVPR is also a recognition of the research team and the depth of the work they’re doing.
